bill.name: Stronger Start for Working Families Act
bill.analyzed: Analyzed the introduced text supplied for S. 3596, focused on section 2 amendments to Internal Revenue Code section 24 affecting the refundable child tax credit earned income threshold, conforming amendment, and effective date.

provisions.title: Section 2
provisions.heading: Earned income threshold for refundable child tax credit
provisions.quote: 2. Earned income threshold for refundable child tax credit (a) In general Section 24(d)(1)(B)(i)  of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended by striking  $3,000  and inserting  $1 . (b) Conforming amendment Section 24(h) of such Code is amended by striking paragraph (6). (c) Effective date The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
goals: Expand access to the refundable child tax credit for taxpayers with earned income below the current threshold.
Increase after-tax resources for low-earning working families with qualifying children.
Reduce child poverty or material hardship among affected households.

effects.text: The bill replaces the permanent $3,000 amount in section 24(d)(1)(B)(i) with $1 and repeals section 24(h)(6), which currently overrides that amount with $2,500. The operative earned-income threshold would therefore fall from $2,500 to $1 for otherwise eligible taxpayers; the 15 percent phase-in rate and refundable cap remain unchanged.
If eligible families file returns and claim the credit, the statutory change could increase refundable credit amounts paid to low-earning households after tax filing.
Larger refundable credit eligibility could increase federal outlays or reduce receipts relative to current law, with the realized effect depending on take-up, eligibility, and filing behavior.
Families with little earned income may have low filing rates or face documentation barriers, which could dampen the intended benefit even if eligibility expands.

barriers.text: The IRS would need to update forms, instructions, eligibility logic, taxpayer-facing guidance, and processing systems for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Eligible low-earning families would need to file returns, document earned income and qualifying children, and understand the changed refundable credit threshold.
Lowering the threshold may increase the importance of verifying eligibility while avoiding delays or mistaken denials for households newly eligible for refunds.

metrics.text: Annual total amount of Additional Child Tax Credit claimed, as an outcome measure of refundable credit dollars delivered after the threshold change.
metrics.rationale: This is the closest supplied IRS concept for the direct statutory outcome because the bill changes refundability under section 24. It measures dollars claimed rather than the exact marginal increase caused by the bill, so analysis would need a baseline or microsimulation to isolate the proposal's contribution. The ACTC claims comparison forecasts return counts; it does not forecast dollar amounts.

metrics.text: IRS Statistics of Income, Individual Income Tax Returns, Publication 1304 Table 3.3: number of returns claiming the refundable child tax credit for TY2027, reported as millions of returns for the registered ACTC pair.
metrics.rationale: Claims illuminate the take-up mechanism behind the policy, but they are a participation measure and can move because of filing behavior, demographics, or outreach rather than the threshold change alone. It should complement, not replace, dollar and poverty outcomes. The reviewed comparison uses the first official TY2027 print under its existing 2029 release window and December 31, 2029 outer deadline; that window is a registered bound, not an announced exact release day.

metrics.text: Census Bureau Supplemental Poverty Measure child poverty rate for CY2027, as a recurring official outcome that reflects refundable tax credits.
metrics.rationale: The SPM is a more relevant poverty metric than broad labor or inflation series because refundable tax credits affect after-tax resources. It is annual and population-wide, so it may be too coarse to detect this bill alone and cannot identify eligible families below the former earned income threshold without additional microdata. The existing registration commits an August 1 through December 31, 2028 release window and December 31, 2028 outer deadline. Its Census announcement authenticates methodology identity, not these lab-committed timing bounds.

metrics.text: No official series separates ACTC claims by earnings band at the threshold margin in a timely publication; SOI tabulations by AGI band are the closest proxy and lag by about two years.
metrics.rationale: Recorded as a gap rather than omitted: the sharpest test of this provision would be claims among families earning under $2,500, and no official publication isolates that band on a useful timeline. Stating the missing series is part of the analysis — it is the demand signal a registry would need to close.

conditionals: P(IRS SOI TY2027 ACTC returns | §24(d)(1)(B)(i) threshold ≤ $1 for TY2027 vs unchanged $2,500 current-law threshold for TY2027; an intermediate enacted threshold is outside both arms)
P(Census SPM child poverty rate for CY2027 | §24(d)(1)(B)(i) threshold ≤ $1 for TY2027 vs unchanged $2,500 current-law threshold for TY2027; an intermediate enacted threshold is outside both arms)
provisions.context: Under current law the refundable portion of the child tax credit (the additional child tax credit) phases in at 15 percent of earned income above a threshold — $3,000 in the permanent statute at §24(d)(1)(B)(i), overridden to $2,500 by §24(h)(6). The bill lowers the permanent threshold to $1 and strikes the $2,500 override, so the phase-in starts from the first dollar of earned income. The 15 percent phase-in rate and the refundable cap are unchanged; the change takes effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

compute.result_summary: Gains concentrate in the lowest income deciles (decile 1 averages +$32/yr vs +$0.30 for decile 10); Gini falls 0.02%. The annual cost declines from $1.86B to $1.53B across the window as earnings growth lifts families past the old $2,500 floor. State income-tax revenue falls about $0.35M per year — itemized separately and excluded from the federal figures above.
